title: Man. Post. Cap. III: Minus commode — culpa unius / poena omnibus; imputation absurdities
pass_a_gloss: Less conveniently you had said the same Cap. 1: this guilt was of one man, but the penalty is common to all men, etc. You observe this distinction between Adam's guilt and the penalty, that the guilt was of one man, but the penalty truly common to all. Do you not see what follows, namely that the penalty does not answer to the guilt; seeing that a guilt that is not common is avenged by a common penalty: a penalty is inflicted on those whose guilt it is not. Certainly if the penalty is of all, the guilt of only one, all except one are free of guilt—how then are they punished justly? If the guilt is of one man and is not common to all, why is it imputed to all? If you say that, though it is of one, it becomes common to all by imputation, you will not escape: first, what is not my guilt ought not to be imputed to me. For it is not imputed to me so that it may become mine, but on the contrary because it is mine, therefore it is imputed to me: otherwise it is imputed to me falsely and unjustly. Next, if Adam's guilt is not mine except by imputation, God the Judge (I shudder thinking it) made me a sinner by His imputation; He did not find me one: for imputation is an act of the judge, not mine. Take away imputation, and I am free of that guilt; for it is not mine, but was of one man, Adam: therefore me (see whither this imputation leads, and shudder with me) the judge, that is, God, made a sinner and guilty, and is the cause of my first sin, of my first reatus. Finally in law Adam's penalty no more belongs to me than his guilt. If therefore his guilt is not mine in the thing itself, but only by imputation, the same must be said of the penalty too.
pass_b_english: You had put the same point less happily in chapter 1: this guilt belonged to one man, but the penalty is common to all. You mark a split between Adam's guilt and the penalty—guilt of one, penalty of all. Do you not see what follows? The penalty then fails to match the guilt: a guilt that is not common is avenged by a common penalty, and punishment falls on people who have no guilt.

If the penalty is everyone's and the guilt only one man's, then all but one are guiltless—how are they justly punished? If the guilt is one man's and not common, why impute it to all? Say that though it is one man's, imputation makes it common to all, and you still do not escape. What is not my guilt ought not to be imputed to me. Imputation does not make it mine so that it can then be charged; rather, because it is mine, it is charged. Otherwise the charge is false and unjust.

And if Adam's guilt is mine only by imputation, then God the Judge—I shudder to think it—made me a sinner by His act of imputing; He did not find me one. Imputation is the judge's act, not mine. Strip away imputation and I am free of that guilt; it is not mine, but was Adam's alone. So the judge—that is, God—made me sinner and guilty (see where this imputation leads, and shudder with me), and becomes the cause of my first sin and first reatus. In law Adam's penalty belongs to me no more than his guilt. If his guilt is not mine in the thing itself, but only by imputation, the same must be said of the penalty.
source_text: Minus commode idem dixeras Cap. 1. haec culpa unius hominis fuit, sed poena omnibus hominibus est communis &c. Hoc discrimen observas inter culpam Adami & poenam, quod culpa unius hominis fuit, poena vero communis omnibus. Nonne vides quid sequatur, nimirum poenam non respondere culpae; quippe, culpam enim non communem vindicari poena communi: poenam iis irrogari, quorum non sit culpa. Certe si poena est omnium, culpa tantum unius, omnes, uno excepto, culpa vacant, quomodo igitur puniuntur juste? Si culpa unius hominis est, nec est communis omnibus, cur omnibus imputatur? Si eam dicas, cum unius sit, imputatione fieri communem omnibus, non evades, primum enim quae mea culpa non est, ea mihi imputari non debet. Non enim ideo mihi imputatur ut sit mea, sed contra quia mea est, idcirco mihi imputatur: alioqui mihi imputatur falso & injuste. Deinde si culpa Adami mea non est nisi imputatione, fecit me Deus Judex (cogitans horresco) sua imputatione peccatorem, non invenit: est enim imputatio judicis actus, non meus. Tolle imputationem, culpa illa vaco; mea enim non est, sed fuit unius hominis Adami: me igitur (vide quo ducat ista imputatio & mecum cohorresce) judex, hoc est, Deus fecit peccatorem ac reum, & causa est primi mei peccati, primi mei reatus. Denique de jure non magis ad me poena Adami pertinet quam culpa. Si igitur culpa ejus mea non est reipsa, sed tantum imputatione, idem etiam de poena dicendum est.
